title: Evaluating nursing performance in heatwave simulations
official: Evaluating nursing performance under environmental stress: a repeated measures cohort study
summary:
Background and study aims
Many healthcare workers in the UK are now working in increasingly hot conditions due to climate change. Heatwaves are becoming more common, and many hospitals do not have full air conditioning. While the effects of heat on patients are well known, less is understood about how working in hot environments affects healthcare staff. High temperatures can increase fatigue and may affect the ability to carry out important clinical tasks safely.
This study aims to test a protocol developed to better understand how heat affects healthcare workers during everyday nursing activities. A specially controlled room (climatic chamber) will be used where temperature conditions can be safely adjusted. Participants will complete a series of simulated nursing tasks under different temperature conditions. Researchers will measure fatigue, physical strain and task performance.
The findings will help determine whether this protocol can be used to assess the impact of heat on healthcare workers and support the development of safer working environments and strategies to protect staff and patients during hot weather.
This research project has been reviewed and approved by the Faculty Research Ethics Committees and the Research Ethics and Governance Office, University of Southampton.

Who can participate?
Physically active volunteer qualified nurses aged 18 to 65 years. 

What does the study involve?
Individuals who meet the study requirements, as determined through a screening health questionnaire, may be eligible to take part. The questionnaire contains general, non-intrusive questions, and all information provided will be treated confidentially. Participants will be asked to attend between three and five visits to the research laboratory in the Clinical Academic Facility (South Block) at Southampton General Hospital. Visits must be separated by at least 48 hours. Each testing session will last approximately 2 hours and 45 minutes, giving a total time commitment of around 9–14 hours.
Participants will be asked to complete three testing sessions and will then have the option of taking part in a further two sessions. Before taking part, participants will complete a consent form. Participation is voluntary and participants may withdraw from the study at any time.

First session
During the first visit, researchers will explain the study procedures and answer any questions. Participants who wish to take part will complete consent forms and health questionnaires. Height and weight will be recorded. The testing procedures will be explained in detail, and participants will have the opportunity to become familiar with the equipment before testing begins.

All sessions
All sessions will follow the same format. The only differences will be the environmental conditions in the climate chamber (18°C, 26°C or 34°C) and whether a cooling intervention, such as a fan, is available.
Three to four hours before arriving at the laboratory, participants will swallow a temperature-sensing pill to measure core body temperature.
At the start of each session, participants will be fitted with monitoring equipment, including:

A soft heart-rate strap worn around the chest
Four small sensors (approximately the size of a 1p coin) attached to the calf, thigh, shoulder and chest

Participants will then enter the climate chamber and complete two assessments of fatigue:
A brief questionnaire about how tired they feel
A 3-minute computer task measuring reaction time

Participants will then cycle on a stationary bike at a low, comfortable pace for 30 minutes. During cycling, they will complete simple cognitive tasks, including basic mathematics and word-colour matching exercises.
Following this, participants will repeat the fatigue assessments before beginning a simulated nursing scenario.
The nursing simulation will take place in the climate chamber, which will be set up to resemble a hospital side room. During the simulation:

A member of the research team will act as different patients
Participants will receive a handover describing six patients
Participants will complete a simulated ward round, including checking observations and administering medications

At two points during the scenario, participants will respond to a simulated cardiac arrest by performing CPR on a training manikin.
Performance during the simulation will be assessed by a researcher using an OSCE-style checklist.
After the simulation, participants will complete the two fatigue assessments again. Once all tasks have been completed, participants will leave the climate chamber and the monitoring equipment will be removed.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There are no direct benefits to participants. However, participation will contribute to research investigating how heat affects healthcare workers and may help inform the development of safer working environments and strategies to protect staff and patients during periods of hot weather.

Participants will be exposed to different temperature conditions in a climate chamber and may experience fatigue or physical strain associated with the study activities. Monitoring equipment will be worn throughout testing sessions, and core temperature will be measured using an ingestible temperature-sensing pill.

Where is the study run from?
The study is being conducted at the research laboratory in the Clinical Academic Facility at Southampton General Hospital, University of Southampton, UK.

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
January 2027 to January 2030.

Who is funding the study?
National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), UK.

Who is the main contact?
Prof Davide Filingeri, D.Filingeri@soton.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Capable of providing informed consent
2. Willing and able to attend all visits 
3. Healthy human volunteers
4. Aged 18-65 years
5. Physically active (i.e. performing 30 minutes regular exercise of moderate intensity, physical activity on at least 3 days each week for at least 3 months)
6. Qualified nurse
Exclusion criteria:
1. Female participant is pregnant
2. Family history of cardiovascular disease
3. Suffering from neurological conditions
4. Suffering from skin conditions (e.g. eczema)
5. Presence of conditions altering thermoregulation and blood flow (e.g. Raynaud’s disease)
6. Smoker or vaper
7. Allergic to adhesives 
8. History of gastrointestinal obstruction, dysphagia, swallowing difficulties
